::: {.lead}
The managers of Byte Bay have money for **one** new platform for *Pocket
Quest* this year: PC, console or cloud gaming. Everyone in the team has an
opinion. "Console players spend the most!" says one. "PC is easy, we
already use the engine!" says another. Opinions are not enough: the
managers want a comparison with clear criteria, numbers and a
recommendation. In lecture 23 you learned the four kinds of gaming
platforms. In this seminar you **compare** them for one game, see how the
specifications of the devices change the performance, and write a
recommendation. Every section ends with a task, and at the end you have a
one-page platform comparison.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary comparison-criteria system-requirements graphics-settings bottleneck decision-matrix porting certification cross-save >}}

## 24.1 Criteria for the comparison

A fair comparison starts with **criteria**, chosen before you look at the
scores (@fig-criteria).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 24.1 — Criteria for comparing platforms"}
Typical criteria for a game:

- **Reach:** how many players can buy and play it on this platform.
- **Fit for the game:** controls, screen and session length.
- **Cost and time:** dev kits, porting work, store fees.
- **Performance:** CPU, GPU and memory of the devices.
- **Testing:** how many devices and settings must be tested.
- **Business model:** premium, free-to-play or subscription.

Take facts from **reliable sources**: the developer pages of the platform
makers and stores, and market reports with a date.
:::

![Criteria for comparing platforms.](images/criteria.png){#fig-criteria width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 24.1 — Opinions become criteria"}
1. "Console players spend the most!" becomes the criterion **business
   model**, checked with a dated market report.
2. "PC is easy, we already use the engine!" becomes **cost and time**,
   checked by listing the porting work.
3. "Our players race on the bus" becomes **fit for the game**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Choosing the criteria after looking at the platforms, so that the favourite
wins. Write the criteria and their weights first, then score.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your criteria"}
Choose a game you know. Write five criteria for choosing its next platform
and say why each one matters for this game.

*Your result:* five criteria with one reason each.
:::

## 24.2 Specifications and performance

The same game must run on devices with very different **specifications**
(@fig-targets).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 24.2 — Specs, settings and requirements"}
The **GPU, CPU and memory** of a device decide how fast it can draw each
frame. A higher setting costs more work per frame: on a weak GPU the frame
rate falls. If the **memory** is too small for a setting, the game
stutters. The weakest part is the **bottleneck**. A studio therefore:

- sets a **target** per platform (resolution, frame rate, memory,
  download size);
- offers **graphics settings** on PC;
- publishes **system requirements:** the **minimum** (low settings, the
  weakest supported device) and the **recommended** (high settings).
:::

![Pocket Quest: targets per platform (example values).](images/targets.png){#fig-targets width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 24.2 — Four PCs, one game"}
With example GPU points (low needs 1.5, medium 3, high 6, ultra 10 for
60 fps):

1. **Old laptop** (2 points, 4 GB RAM): low gives 80 fps; medium needs
   6 GB RAM and stutters.
2. **Office PC** (4 points, 8 GB): high gives only 40 fps; the **GPU** is
   the bottleneck. Medium gives 80 fps.
3. **Handheld PC** (6 points, 16 GB): high at 60 fps.
4. **Gaming PC** (12 points, 16 GB): ultra at 72 fps.
5. Minimum: GPU 2 points, 4 GB RAM. Recommended: GPU 6 points, 8 GB RAM.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/spec-compare.html" poster="sims/spec-compare.png" title="Spec Check: will Pocket Quest run well?" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Testing only on the developers' strong PCs. The minimum requirements must
come from a test on the weakest supported device.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the settings"}
1. In **Spec Check**, find the highest setting with 60 fps for each device.
2. Write the minimum and recommended requirements in your own words.

*Your result:* a table of four devices and two requirement lines.
:::

## 24.3 The decision matrix

A **decision matrix** turns the criteria into numbers (@fig-matrix).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 24.3 — Decision matrix"}
1. Write the criteria and give each a **weight** (for example 1 to 3).
2. Give each platform a **score** per criterion (1 to 5, 5 = best), with a
   reason or a source.
3. Multiply score × weight and **add up**. The highest total is the best
   option **for these weights**.
4. Check how the result changes when a weight changes (a **sensitivity
   check**).
:::

![A decision matrix (example scores).](images/decision-matrix.png){#fig-matrix width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 24.3 — The next platform for Pocket Quest"}
1. Weights: reach 3, fit 3, cost and time 2, performance 1, testing 1.
2. Totals: **PC 37**, console 35, cloud 29 (of 50).
3. With equal weights the console wins (19 to 17): the result depends on
   what matters most to Byte Bay.
4. With little money (cost and time 3), PC still leads: 41 to 37.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/decision-matrix.html" poster="sims/decision-matrix.png" title="Decision Matrix: the next platform for Pocket Quest" height="620" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Treating the total as the truth. The scores are estimates; if two options
are only a few points apart, say so, and explain which weight decides.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your matrix"}
1. In **Decision Matrix**, find weights where the console wins with reach at
   2 or more.
2. Make your own matrix for the game you chose in 24.1, with three
   platforms.

*Your result:* a matrix with weights, scores and totals.
:::

## 24.4 From the matrix to a recommendation

The managers want a short **recommendation** with a plan for the port
(@fig-port).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 24.4 — A platform recommendation"}
A one-page recommendation has:

1. **The question** (which platform next, and why now).
2. **The matrix** with weights, scores and sources.
3. **The choice** and the margin, with the result of the sensitivity check.
4. **The porting plan:** controls, menus, graphics settings, accounts and
   saves, store rules, testing on the weakest device.
5. **The risks** and how to reduce them.
:::

![What changes in a port?](images/port-checklist.png){#fig-port width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 24.4 — Byte Bay's recommendation"}
1. *Question:* which platform for *Pocket Quest* this year?
2. *Choice:* **PC** (37 of 50), ahead of the console (35); the console
   wins only if testing matters much more.
3. *Port plan:* keyboard and controller, mouse menus, low to ultra
   settings, cross-save with the same account, requirements on the store
   page.
4. *Risk:* many PC configurations; reduce it with tests on an old laptop
   and an office PC.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A recommendation without the port plan. The cost of the port is often the
biggest surprise: list the work before the decision, not after.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your recommendation"}
Write a one-page recommendation for the game you chose: the question, your
matrix, the choice with its margin, a port plan of five points and one
risk.

*Your result:* a one-page recommendation.
:::

## Case study: Port Planner

The first test builds of *Pocket Quest* bring six reports: 20 fps on an old
laptop; a console menu that says "Tap to start"; a certification report
about an unplugged controller; a PC store page without hardware
requirements; a player who starts the PC version at level 1; and cloud
players at 70 ms ping who feel the car react late. The Game challenge of
the interactive lesson uses these reports. In the mini-game below you
choose the best fix for each one.

{{< sim file="sims/port-planner.html" poster="sims/port-planner.png" title="Port Planner: fix the test reports" kind="game" height="480" >}}

## Further reading

Novak, *Game Development Essentials* (3rd ed., 2012), Chapter 1. The
"system requirements" sections of PC store pages and the developer pages
of the platform makers show real targets and rules.

## Exercises

1. Name four criteria for comparing gaming platforms.
2. Why must the criteria and weights be written before the scores?
3. What is a bottleneck?
4. What do the minimum and the recommended requirements describe?
5. A device has GPU 4 points; high needs 6 points for 60 fps. About how
   many fps does it reach on high?
6. What happens when the memory is too small for a setting?
7. How do you compute the total of a platform in a decision matrix?
8. PC scores 4, 4, 4, 3, 2 with weights 3, 3, 2, 1, 1. What is the total?
9. What is a sensitivity check?
10. Name four points of a porting plan.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. For example reach, fit for the game, cost and time, performance,
   testing, business model.
2. So that the favourite does not win just because the criteria were made
   for it.
3. The weakest part of a system, which limits the performance.
4. Minimum: the weakest supported device, low settings. Recommended: a
   device that runs high settings well.
5. 60 × 4 / 6 = 40 fps.
6. The game stutters (for example the frame rate halves).
7. Multiply each score by its weight and add up.
8. 12 + 12 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 37.
9. Changing a weight to see whether the winner changes.
10. For example controls, menus, graphics settings, accounts and saves,
    store rules, testing.
:::
